    <title>Tolerance measured at one developmental stage mispredicts climate resilience in an animal with a complex life cycle</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3004079" title="Tolerance measured at one developmental stage mispredicts climate resilience in an animal with a complex life cycle" />

    <content type="html"><p>by Hao Song, Tingyu Shi, Meijie Yang, Xiaoyan Liu, Zhuoqing Li, Pu Shi, Yu Wu, Bassem Allam, Andrew Jeffs, Bradley Skelton, Tao Zhang</p>

Forecasts of whether marine species can evolve fast enough to survive climate change rely largely on single-stage tolerance assays, tacitly assuming that tolerance measured at one developmental stage reflects adaptive capacity across the organism’s life cycle. We test this assumption in a common marine bivalve (<i>Mercenaria mercenaria</i>) and find that it fails in sign, not degree: larval and post-metamorphic tolerance to end-century ocean acidification are strongly negatively correlated (<i>r</i> = −0.53, 95% CI [−0.69, −0.33]) across family-level, pedigree-conditioned and animal model estimates, with pervasive rank reversals among the top performers of each stage. A multivariate analysis of the among-family covariance matrix G shows why: under acidification, 57% of the among-family variance collapses onto a single dominant axis that loads positively on every larval trait and negatively on every post-metamorphic trait, whereas under ambient conditions the same families show no cross-stage covariance at all. Acidification therefore does not merely depress performance—it reorganizes the genetic architecture into a cross-stage conflict. Under ramping RCP 8.5 forcing this conflict geometry dictates the direction—not merely the magnitude—of adaptation: only balanced multi-stage selection preserves family diversity, whereas single-stage selection systematically erodes the opposite axis. In complex life cycles, resilience is a geometric property of ontogeny that forecasts cannot compress into a single-stage without inverting the sign of the answer.</content>

    <title>High-resolution paleobiome reconstructions highlight ecological and historical dynamics underpinning global terrestrial vertebrate diversity</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3004077" title="High-resolution paleobiome reconstructions highlight ecological and historical dynamics underpinning global terrestrial vertebrate diversity" />

    <content type="html"><p>by Alexander Skeels, Julian Rogger, Marcel Cardillo, Alexander Farnsworth, Daniel J. Lunt, Dirk Nikolaus Karger</p>

Past climate change has repeatedly reshaped Earth’s biomes, yet how their expansion and contraction influence biodiversity patterns through time remains unclear. Competing hypotheses propose that either historical biome area has a strong influence on diversity, or that biodiversity responds rapidly to environmental change, such that present-day biome area and energy are sufficient to explain diversity patterns. Progress in testing these ideas has been limited by sparse and inconsistent proxy data and the coarse resolution of existing paleoclimate models. Here, we reconstructed global biome histories for the Cenozoic (66–0 Ma) by downscaling five different paleoclimate simulations. Estimates of change in biome area through time were generally consistent among alternative climate models and with the empirical proxy record. Accounting for variation among models, we found that present-day area and energy were consistently better predictors of vertebrate diversity than historical measures. These findings suggest biodiversity tracks the ecological limits set by shifting biomes, leaving sparse legacy of past dynamics. Our results highlight the importance of integrating multiple paleoclimate reconstructions when assessing the historical drivers of biodiversity.</content>

    <title>Host–virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3003836" title="Host–virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3003836.PDF" title="(PDF) Host–virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation" />

    <published>2026-10-22T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Aleksei Belyi, Yiyang Du, Alastair J. Wilson, Ben Longdon, Francis M. Jiggins</p>

Host–parasite coevolution is expected to generate strong selection for resistance and infectivity that has the potential to erode genetic variation. Despite this, natural populations often retain extensive genetic variation in these traits. Genotype-by-genotype interactions on fitness can generate negative frequency-dependent selection, which helps maintain this variation by preventing any host or pathogen genotype from retaining a permanent advantage. Because these interactions place genetic variance in the interaction term rather than in additive differences among hosts or pathogens, that variance is masked from directional selection and can remain ‘cryptic’. Here we combine coevolutionary modelling with large‑scale experimental infection assays to quantify how host-pathogen interactions structure fitness variance in a vertically transmitted virus system, <i>Drosophila melanogaster</i> and sigma virus. Simulations show that coevolution typically erodes additive genetic variance in host and pathogen fitness, concentrating variance in host-virus interaction terms. Consistent with these predictions, experiments spanning 90 host-virus genotype combinations reveal that transmission, viral load, and virulence are overwhelmingly governed by host-virus genetic interactions rather than host or virus main effects. As a result, neither host resistance alleles nor viral genotypes confer consistently higher fitness across genetic backgrounds. Interactions tend to be sex‑specific, further limiting heritable fitness variation. Our results demonstrate that coevolution can substantially mask heritable genetic variation from directional selection by rendering fitness context-dependent. This extensive cryptic genetic variation may be revealed either when ecological or evolutionary conditions shift, or when the process of coevolution itself alters the direction of selection. This demonstrates the need to account for genotype-specific interactions when forecasting evolutionary responses.</content>

    <title>A cortical semantic map integrates fractions and integers in the human brain</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3003820" title="A cortical semantic map integrates fractions and integers in the human brain" />

    <content type="html"><p>by Daniela Valério, Samuel Debray, Alireza Karami, Maxime Cauté, Nicolás Gravel, Stanislas Dehaene</p>

How does the human brain represent the meaning of abstract symbols? Some theories postulate the existence of semantic spaces where concepts occupy positions that reflect their conceptual relationships. In the number domain, psychological evidence suggests that integers are represented along a mental number line which, with education, integrates higher-level number concepts such as fractions. To test this hypothesis, we recorded whole-brain 7T fMRI responses to integer and fraction symbols during an active magnitude comparison task designed to engage magnitude processing. Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.</content>

    <title>Non-adaptive evolutionary forces predominantly shape nucleotide composition near human transcription start sites</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3004063" title="Non-adaptive evolutionary forces predominantly shape nucleotide composition near human transcription start sites" />
    <link rel="related" type="application/pdf" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article/asset?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3004063.PDF" title="(PDF) Non-adaptive evolutionary forces predominantly shape nucleotide composition near human transcription start sites" />

      <name>Fanny Pouyet</name>

      <name>Alexander F. Palazzo</name>

    <published>2026-10-21T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Yi Qiu, Emilie Hebraud, Fanny Pouyet, Alexander F. Palazzo</p>

In the human genome, mutation rates vary along genes, yet how their fine-scale structure contributes to gene evolution has remained largely unexplored. Here, we map inherited mutations at single-nucleotide resolution and uncover a striking hypermutation peak at transcription start sites (TSSs) of human protein-coding genes. This pattern is observed both in population polymorphisms and in de novo mutations from parent-offspring trios, and is dependent on transcriptional activity in testes. We also find similar hypermutation peaks at TSSs used to produce long noncoding RNAs and at intergenic RNA Polymerase II pause sites. In addition, we identify distinct mutational signatures at exon-intron boundaries and in introns. By comparing the current nucleotide content to predicted equilibrium levels, inferred from mutation and fixation rates, and by analyzing derived ancestral frequency spectrums, we detect signals that are compatible with a low level of ongoing background GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) throughout the region and ancestral elevated gBGC activity that is centered right downstream from the TSS. Using a forward-in-time simulation algorithm, we show that the current nucleotide composition surrounding the TSS of protein-coding genes is best explained by local mutation biases coupled to ongoing and ancestral patterns of gene conversions. Our simulations allow us to infer several features of these gBGC events. Overall, these findings indicate that the nucleotide composition around TSSs is largely shaped by non-adaptive forces, particularly mutation bias and gBGC.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Huimin Liu, Yuzhen Wang, Ruiqing Yu, Kexin Liu, Dezhi Zheng, Bo Wang, Yuan Chang, Bing Liu, Xuetian Yue, Zhuanchang Wu, Chunyang Li, Xiaohong Liang, Chunhong Ma, Guohua Liu, Jianhua Li, Leiqi Xu, Lifen Gao</p>

Macrophages play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing molecule 4 (TIMD4) is involved in the regulation of tissue-resident macrophages. TIMD4 expression is elevated in colonic tissues from patients with ulcerative colitis (UC) and mice with dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis, but its role in IBD pathogenesis remains unclear. In this study, we found that <i>Timd4</i> deficiency aggravated DSS-induced colitis, accompanied by increased infiltration of monocytes into the colonic tissues. Treatment with a CCR2 antagonist attenuated colonic inflammation and reduced monocyte infiltration into colonic tissues in <i>Timd4</i> KO mice. Mechanistically, in vitro studies revealed that TIMD4 stabilized the LKB1-STRAD-MO25 complex via its intracellular domain, thereby activating the AMPK pathway and suppressing NF-κB-dependent chemokine production in macrophages. Based on these findings, we designed a TIMD4-derived peptide and developed a macrophage-targeted nanoparticle system (T4<sub>(365–378)</sub>‑NPs). Treatment with T4<sub>(365–378)</sub>-NPs reduced P65 phosphorylation and attenuated DSS-induced colitis in mice. Treatment with either T4<sub>(365–378)</sub>-NPs or the CCR2 antagonist attenuated DSS-induced colitis, and no statistically significant differences in the assessed outcomes were detected between the two groups. Administration of T4<sub>(365–378)</sub>-NPs before DSS exposure also attenuated subsequent colitis. Furthermore, combining the T4<sub>(365–378)</sub>‑NPs with anti-α4β7 or anti-TNF-α antibodies produced greater improvements than either monotherapy in the DSS-induced colitis model. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of TIMD4-derived peptide delivery as a potential therapeutic approach for intestinal inflammation.</content>

    <title>Oxidative signaling thresholds shape vulnerability in the central and peripheral nervous systems</title>
    <link rel="alternate" href="https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3004032" title="Oxidative signaling thresholds shape vulnerability in the central and peripheral nervous systems" />

    </author>

    <updated>2026-10-19T14:00:00Z</updated>
    <published>2026-10-19T14:00:00Z</published>
    <content type="html"><p>by Shuji Wakatsuki, Toshiyuki Araki</p>

Neurodegeneration is frequently associated with oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms that convert reactive oxygen species (ROS) into irreversible degenerative signals remain incompletely understood. Neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems often differ in their responses to injury, but these differences cannot be reduced to a simple contrast between weak and strong antioxidant capacity. This Essay proposes that neuronal vulnerability is shaped by multilayered signaling thresholds comprising ROS production, antioxidant and thiol buffering, redox-sensitive signal detection, molecular gating, and commitment to degeneration, survival, or repair. This framework may help explain selective neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases and identify intervention points downstream of global ROS suppression.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Chang Ye, Yan-Yu Zang, Gui-Fang Duan, Jiang Chen, Dan Wu, Dan Wang, Changlin Li, Yun Xu, Tianjiao Xia, Xiaoping Gu, Yun Stone Shi</p>

In mammals, heat sensation is primarily mediated by thermosensitive channels, particularly transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons. However, whether additional channels contribute to noxious heat detection remains unclear. Here, we investigated the role of the mechanosensitive cation channel TMEM63B in DRG neurons and unexpectedly discovered its involvement in noxious thermosensation rather than mechanosensation. TMEM63B was broadly expressed in DRG neurons, and its global knockout or DRG-specific conditional knockout markedly reduced heat sensitivity. Deletion of TMEM63B significantly attenuated heat-induced calcium responses and currents in DRG neurons and elevated the temperature threshold for action potential initiation. Recombinant TMEM63B exhibited moderate heat response in calcium imaging assays. Notably, in the presence of arachidonic acid, TMEM63B was strongly activated by heat, suggesting that its thermosensitivity is modulated by the membrane lipid environment. Together, these findings identify TMEM63B as a novel channel contributing to heat sensation and reveal a lipid-dependent modulation of its channel activity.</content>

<i>Agrobacterium</i>-mediated transient expression has revolutionised plant research, enabling numerous landmark discoveries across diverse areas of plant biology. Yet this powerful approach remains largely confined to solanaceous species, leaving most economically important crop families without a comparable rapid assay platform. Here, we show that an engineered <i>Rhizobium rhizogenes</i> strain, AS109, mediates efficient transient expression across diverse dicot species spanning multiple taxonomic families, consistently outperforming commonly used laboratory agrobacterial strains. Leveraging the broad host range of AS109, we establish a suite of functional assays in faba bean (<i>Vicia faba</i>), including protein localisation, RNA interference-mediated gene silencing, cell-surface elicitor recognition screens, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor (NLR) activation, and infection cell biology at the host-pathogen interface. AS109 thus provides an accessible and versatile chassis for functional genomics in non-model crops, bridging the widening gap between hypothesis generation and experimental validation across diverse plant species.</content>

Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is a major cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, yet its underlying mechanism remains elusive. Here, we show that growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) levels are significantly reduced in the placenta and fetal circulation in mouse and pig FGR models and correlate positively with fetal weight. Placenta-specific GDF15 deficiency causes FGR, while placenta-specific <i>Gdf15</i> mRNA delivery through targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) effectively alleviates FGR. Mechanistically, placental GDF15 is a major contributor to the fetal circulating GDF15 pool and enters the fetal compartment, where it activates the hepatic STAT3 signaling pathway to stimulate IGF2 production during pregnancy. Placental GDF15 deficiency decreases hepatic STAT3 phosphorylation and IGF2 levels in fetuses. Inhibition of STAT3 in primary mouse fetal hepatocytes blocks GDF15-induced IGF2 upregulation. Placenta-specific <i>Gdf15</i> mRNA-LNP administration rescues the decreased hepatic p-STAT3 and IGF2 levels in FGR fetuses. Collectively, our findings identify a placenta-fetal liver metabolic axis where placental GDF15 promotes fetal growth by activating the fetal hepatic STAT3-IGF2 pathway, revealing a potential therapeutic target for FGR.</content>

Barrier epithelia are shielded from the external environment by their apical extracellular matrices (aECMs). The molecular complexity of aECMs has challenged understanding of their organization in vivo. To define the molecular architecture of a model aECM we generated a toolkit of 105 fluorescently tagged aECM components using gene editing in <i>C. elegans</i>, focusing on proteins secreted by the epidermis to form the collagen-rich cuticle. We developed efficient pipelines for modular protein tagging and rapid fluorophore swapping. We define multiple reference markers for key substructures including the little-understood cortical layer, as well as the helical crossed fiber arrays that function as a hydrostatic skeleton to maintain organismal shape. Social learning is a fundamental adaptive strategy that critically shapes decision-making and feeding behaviors. Through the social transmission of food preference (STFP), animals acquire information about food safety via social interactions, forming a food-odor memory that overrides innate preferences and guides subsequent food preferences. However, the neural mechanisms through which social cues durably influence feeding preferences remain unclear. Here, we identify the lateral septum (LS) as a key node in STFP. We show that LS neuronal activity increases following social learning and reliably distinguishes between socially cued and uncued foods. Chemogenetic inhibition of the dorsal LS (dLS), but not the ventral LS (vLS), abolishes STFP-driven food preference, revealing subregional specificity within the LS. Furthermore, oxytocin receptor (OXTR) signaling within the dLS is required for STFP in mice, where it enhances neuronal excitability through PLC pathway activation. Together, our results reveal a subregion-specific circuit mechanism through which the dLS integrates social information with feeding motivation, and highlight oxytocinergic modulation as a key mediator of socially guided food preferences.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Qiaoli Huang, Christian F. Doeller</p>

Human cognition is capacity-limited, requiring strategies to actively structure information. Eye movements offer a natural mechanism for sequential sampling, but whether such sequences reflect memory organization is unknown. We developed a working-memory task where color-frequency pairings created a latent ordinal structure to optimally reduce memory load. Across two experiments, gaze patterns spontaneously aligned with this structure. Participants sampled items following this sequence during encoding and revisited them during maintenance. Critically, the expression of this structure depended on cognitive demand. In a 3-item task, high performers showed robust sequential sampling during encoding, whereas lower performers compensated with replay-like revisitation during maintenance. Under higher demand (4 items), encoding-based organization was disrupted, and structured revisitation emerged primarily during maintenance. These findings suggest that eye movements provide an overt expression of an internally generated organizational process that flexibly adapts to cognitive demands, revealing a behavioral analogue to neural replay when encoding resources are strained.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Steven Moran, Tiena Danner, Marcia S. Ponce de León, Christoph P. E. Zollikofer</p>

Human vocal tracts, like other physical traits, exhibit extensive interindividual variation. However, little is known about how this variation translates into phonetic diversity between speakers, and ultimately, across languages. Here we develop a biocultural model of phonetic evolution, analogous to Russell Lande’s model of multivariate phenotypic evolution. We show that individual vocal tract morphologies and associated articulatory strategies leave consistent acoustic signatures, resulting in a characteristic pattern of phonetic variation within speaker groups that correlates with the pattern observed between groups. Recalling a central tenet of evolutionary biology—that within-group variation feeds between-group diversification—our findings suggest that phonologically similar vowel systems can attain phonetically diverse realizations according to a neutral-like evolutionary process. Our model serves as a null hypothesis for disentangling the biological versus cultural mechanisms underlying phonetic diversification, where deviations from the neutral expectation may indicate culturally mediated language change.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Mohammadjavad Meghrazi, Sarah P. Otto</p>

Many traits divert resources from reproduction and are costly due to the physiological trade-offs organisms face. These traits might require the allocation of different resources, e.g., energy expenditure or production of macromolecules, and it is unclear how their costs can be compared given their different units. Moreover, the effect of environmental conditions and genetic background on the cost of traits is not well understood. Two different frameworks have been proposed to quantify the resource costs of traits, focusing on either energy allocation or proteome allocation. These frameworks implicitly assume energy provisioning or protein production limits growth, respectively, but the connection between the two limitations has been underexplored. To better connect these frameworks, we develop a framework that considers limitations in energy provisioning and macromolecule biosynthesis simultaneously to quantify and compare the cost of traits that require different resources. Using this model, we explore how environmental quality and genetic background affect the cost of traits. Notably, our model predicts that increasing food quality increases the cost of traits that require the production of new structures, while decreasing the cost of traits requiring energy expenditure. Moreover, our model makes novel predictions about the effect of degradation, recycling, and energetic demands for maintenance on the relationship between the macromolecular composition of the cells and growth rate (also known as bacterial growth laws).</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Edith Sánchez, Khalid Sedeek, Haroon Butt, Magdy Mahfouz</p>

Precise, site-specific integration of large DNA sequences into plant genomes is a long-standing goal of crop biotechnology and synthetic biology, yet remains constrained by random insertion, inefficient homologous recombination, and gene targeting. Here, we present PrimeStack, a DSB-independent platform that integrates PE with the unidirectional large serine integrase Bxb1, leveraging evolved variants for enhanced activity, to achieve the programmable insertion of multigene, multikilobase cargos at predefined genomic safe harbors (GSH) in rice (<i>Oryza sativa</i>). Optimized prime editors first install <i>attP</i> landing sites with high fidelity and heritability followed by Bxb1-mediated recombination that generates irreversible integration of genetic information. PrimeStack enabled targeted large-cargo integration in regenerated rice plants with efficiencies of up to 45%, as determined by junction-specific PCR analyses. No obvious morphological differences from WT plants were observed at 5 weeks after transfer to soil under the evaluated conditions. We validate its utility by achieving targeted insertion of a carotenoid cassette at an experimentally confirmed genomic safe harbor. PrimeStack delivers a modular, site-specific gene stacking platform that enables predictable, multigene trait pyramiding and pathway construction at GSH, thereby accelerating the development of improved and resilient crop varieties, as well as scalable plant-based biomanufacturing and a powerful chassis for synthetic biology.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Yina Wang, Robert J. Tancer, Maggie Wear, Katrina M. Jackson, Yu Zhang, Kan Li, Jun Wang, Yong-Gui Gao, Kirsten Nielsen, Arturo Casadevall, Chaoyang Xue</p>

Nutrient sensing and utilization are critical for microbes to adapt to their environment and evade predators. The encapsuled yeast <i>Cryptococcus neoformans</i> has a unique ability to sense and utilize the sugar inositol as both a signaling molecule and as a carbon source. This trait is advantageous not only in the natural environment but also to promote its pathogenesis, including invasion of the central nervous system. In this study, we have identified a novel inositol transporter-like receptor (transceptor) Itr4 that coordinates inositol and glucose metabolism by regulating inositol transporters (<i>ITR</i>s) and glucose sensor Hxs1.     <content type="html"><p>by Zhiru Liu, Benjamin H. Good</p>

The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions (dN/dS) encodes important information about the selection pressures acting on protein-coding genes. In bacterial populations, dN/dS often declines with the sequence divergence between strains, but the mechanisms responsible for this broad empirical trend are still debated. Existing models have primarily focused on de novo mutations, overlooking the older genetic variants that are continually introduced through horizontal gene transfer and recombination. Here we introduce a phenomenological model of dN/dS in recombining populations of bacteria, which allows us to disentangle the effects of recombination among pairs of closely related strains. We find that clonally inherited regions of the genome exhibit consistently higher dN/dS ratios, and that the accumulation of recombined segments can quantitatively explain the majority of the decline in dN/dS. We use these observations to re-examine models of purifying selection and adaptive reversion in human gut bacteria, and uncover evidence for widespread weak selection at a large fraction of protein-coding sites. Our findings show that horizontal gene transfer can be an important factor in shaping genome-wide patterns of selective constraint, and raise new questions about the effectiveness of natural selection in complex bacterial populations.</content>

Fungal morphogenesis is a major driver of disease outcome. For the opportunistic fungal pathogen <i>Cryptococcus neoformans</i>, extreme morphological heterogeneity within the lung environment drives dissemination, immune evasion, and drug resistance. One such cell type is the small, oval, titanide (2–4 µm). This poorly understood cell type is prevalent in lung histology as well as host-relevant in vitro conditions. In conditions that generate cellular heterogeneity, titanides comprise 4%–10% of cells 24 hours post-induction and by 72 hours are the dominant cell type. Despite their prevalence and the significance of cryptococcal morphogenesis for virulence, key questions pertaining to their origin, fate, and underlying biology remain unstudied. Using TEM, SEM, and fluorescence microscopy we demonstrate that titanides display distinct morphological features; they possess thin cell walls, single birth scars, and capsules, with reduced Pathogen-Associated Molecular Pattern exposure and altered distribution. These features distinguish titanides from previously described <i>C. neoformans</i> ‘small cells’ such as in vivo seed cells (6 µm, high cell-wall mannan content) and micro cells (round, <1 μm, with thick cell walls) among others. Using microfluidics, we reveal that titanides arise from yeast-like ‘typical’ mothers, highlighting the morphological plasticity of typical cells in host-relevant conditions. Upon birth, titanides have compact nuclei and do not immediately proliferate, but transfer to fresh media results in rapid swelling and cell division. Consistent with this, titanides are more resistant to some cell wall/membrane stressors and are an effective infectious propagule in a murine model. Together, these findings establish a definition and essential characterisation of the titanide cell type and provide new insight into a key player in <i>C. neoformans</i> cell biology and pathogenesis.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Tianhe Wang, Tony Lam, Jordan A. Taylor, Richard B. Ivry</p>

The sensorimotor system is continuously adjusted to minimize error. Current theories assume that this adaptation process entails the operation of multiple learning systems, with a key division between implicit and explicit components. Recent studies have revealed several inconsistencies regarding the characteristics and constraints of the implicit system, suggesting that the current framework is incomplete. Here, we propose that these conflicting findings can be understood by recognizing that there are multiple implicit subcomponents, each with distinct computational goals. One well-studied component is implicit recalibration, a process critical for action execution which uses sensory-prediction errors to automatically refine the sensorimotor map. In the current study, we describe a second, novel component, implicit aiming, a process which contributes to action selection to achieve specific goals. Through a series of studies using human participants, we find compelling evidence that those two implicit processes show a clear separation in their temporal stabilities and contextual modulations. These distinct properties correspond to different computational frameworks attributing learning dynamics to either contextual inference or cancellation of competing neural populations, respectively. Together, these findings suggest an alternative framework for sensorimotor adaptation based on the computational goals of the system rather than phenomenology.</content>

The ability to monitor the proliferative status of live cells both in vitro and in vivo over time has revolutionised our understanding of development, growth and disease. This was first made possible by fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator (Fucci) technology, which distinguishes specific cell cycle phases through the reciprocal degradation of fluorescently tagged, truncated forms of human CDT1 and GMNN proteins. We show that this system accurately discriminates and permits tracking of cells in G1, S, G2, and M phases both in vitro and in vivo, enabling faithful visualisation of cell cycle status in intact tissues and organs. The cation channel of sperm, CatSper, is a sperm-specific calcium channel essential for male fertility across metazoans. CatSper is activated by intracellular alkalinization, membrane depolarization, and elevated temperature, which together ensure maximal current generation. Together, these results show that distinct click-train temporal patterns are differentially represented across the auditory system, with stronger sensitivity emerging in higher auditory structures.</content>

    <content type="html"><p>by Albin Teulet, Sebastian Schornack</p>

Rhizobia are soil bacteria that establish nitrogen-fixing symbioses with legumes. While many rhizobia use a Type III Secretion System to deliver “Nodulation Outer Protein” (Nop) effectors, some uniquely use these proteins to initiate nodule organogenesis, bypassing classical signalling. The molecular functions of these effectors remain largely unknown due to extreme sequence divergence. Using AlphaFold2-mediated structural proteomics, we identified a modular architecture in rhizobial effectors composed of 22 distinct structural units. We reveal that many Nop effectors are cryptic transcriptional or post-transcriptional regulators, harbouring unrecognised nucleic acid–binding modules and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase domains. Crucially, these modules are conserved in specific plant pathogens, such as gall-inducing <i>Pantoea</i>, where our predicted structural units align with experimentally validated DNA-binding domains. Furthermore, we discovered the BPN (B3 and PUA-like nucleic acid binding) domain as a structural mimic of plant B3-domain transcription factors, pointing to a direct mechanism for hijacking legume development. Our findings strongly suggest that rhizobia employ a modular domain-fusion strategy to act as direct genetic modulators, uncovering a conserved mechanism used by both symbionts and pathogens to hijack host developmental programmes.</content>
